text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:

- Tens of thousands of metalworkers protest against cuts in sick pay. Centre of demonstrations in North Rhine-Westphalia and Baden-Wuerttemberg. Demonstrations recall start of 1956 strike, the longest in West German history, when workers won the demand for full sick pay.
- Berlin coalition agrees budget plans for 1997. Results far from good, but acceptable, says Berlin Mayor Eberhard Diepgen. Assets will be sold and manufacturers' tax raised.
- SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping says Germany under leadership of Chancellor Helmut Kohl is "not fit for future". Kohl has failed to recognise the signs of a social crisis in Germany.
- Kohl to visit Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan. Chancellor plans to discuss human rights, but has no plans to meet opposition leaders.
- Massive protests exacerbate sick pay dispute

- Germany's industrial competitiveness falls further behind other nations, Institut der Deutschen Wirtschaft (IW) survey finds. In last five years German productivity has fallen from third to fifth place, as Japan and France pass Germany.
- Deutsche Bank profits rise, operating profits up 26 percent to 3.5 billion marks
- Deposit for beer cans may be introduced as environmental protection measure.
- German unions say that "hot autumn" has started, some 400,000 metalworkers take part in demonstrations.
- Rubbish collectors in cities and towns will not have to pay value added tax, as feared.
- Labour Minister Norbert Bluem warns unions and employers against divisive fight
- German President Roman Herzog predicts job miracle for Germany in the service sector.
